C005.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with low labor demand elasticity
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with low labor demand elasticity unemployment among low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies of minimum wage increases in U.S. states with low labor demand elasticity (e.g., manufacturing-intensive regions) combined with administrative wage and employment data from 2010-2023 — Provides direct causal evidence on employment effects in the specified market conditions, leveraging variation in enforcement strength and training program availability.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage employment effects focusing on low-elasticity contexts, such as Card & Krueger (1995) replication studies and subsequent updates covering developed countries with strong labor law enforcement — Synthesizes existing findings to assess whether the hypothesized reduction in unemployment holds across multiple settings, accounting for heterogeneous labor demand elasticities.

[PATH:theoretical] Search-and-matching labor market models incorporating minimum wage, monopsony power, and complementary training programs (e.g., models by Manning or Acemoglu & Pischke) — Tests the logical consistency of the hypothesis under low elasticity assumptions and identifies mechanisms (e.g., increased human capital investment) that could explain unemployment reduction.

scope.domain: low labor demand elasticity markets with strong enforcement and complementary training programs

qualifier.geographic: developed countries with strong labor law enforcement

C006.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with low labor demand elasticity
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with low labor demand elasticity employment among low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiment studies of minimum wage increases in geographically bounded urban labor markets with low worker mobility (e.g., city-level wage floors in the United States or Germany) — These studies directly test the hypothesis by exploiting exogenous variation in minimum wage levels in contexts where labor demand elasticity is plausibly low and worker mobility is limited, allowing identification of employment effects among low-skilled workers.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage employment effects stratified by labor demand elasticity estimates (e.g., using industry-level or occupation-level elasticity data from labor economics literature) — A systematic review and meta-regression can assess whether the predicted positive employment effect holds specifically in low-elasticity settings, controlling for economic growth periods and geographic constraints, thereby clarifying the disputed status.

[PATH:theoretical] Dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models incorporating search-and-matching frictions and heterogeneous labor markets with low mobility — Such models can simulate the causal mechanism underlying the hypothesis, isolating the effect of minimum wage changes on low-skilled employment under varying elasticity and mobility assumptions, and providing testable predictions for empirical validation.

qualifier.temporal: during periods of moderate economic growth
qualifier.geographic: in urban labor markets with limited low-skilled worker mobility

C007.subject: Raising the minimum wage to a living wage level
C007.object: employee turnover and increases productivity among low-skilled workers only in firms with high management quality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage to a living wage level employee turnover and increases productivity among low-skilled workers only in firms with high management quality]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental study of minimum wage increases in service industries, matched with management quality scores (e.g., from employer surveys or productivity audits), comparing turnover rates and productivity changes across firms above and below the median management quality threshold. — Directly tests the conditional effect: if the hypothesis holds, we expect significant reductions in turnover and gains in productivity only in firms with high management quality, while no such effects appear in low-management-quality firms. This can confirm or refute the core claim.

[PATH:literature] Literature review and meta-analysis of existing studies on minimum wage effects, stratified by management practices or firm-level organizational capital (e.g., using measures from the Management, Organization, and Innovation (MOI) survey data). — Synthesizes prior evidence to assess whether the hypothesized moderation by management quality is consistently observed across contexts, identifying gaps or contradictory findings that could support or undermine the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation model of low-wage labor markets, incorporating heterogeneous firms with varying management quality and worker turnover dynamics, calibrated to service industry data. — Provides a formal test of the causal mechanism: if high management quality enables better utilization of higher wages (e.g., through training, motivation, or retention), the model should generate the predicted pattern. This can reveal whether the hypothesis is logically coherent under plausible assumptions.

qualifier.condition: when management quality is above the industry median

C008.subject: Raising the minimum wage
C008.object: employee turnover and decreases productivity among low-skilled workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage employee turnover and decreases productivity among low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal firm-level payroll and turnover data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (JOLTS survey) matched with state minimum wage changes — Directly tests whether rapid minimum wage hikes correlate with increased turnover and decreased productivity in high-turnover service industries, using objective administrative data.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled field experiments in retail and fast-food chains, randomly assigning wage increases to certain stores while keeping others as controls — Provides causal evidence on the short-term effects of wage hikes on employee retention and productivity, avoiding confounding factors common in observational studies.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on minimum wage effects on labor market outcomes, focusing on worker turnover and productivity in low-skilled service sectors — Synthesizes findings across multiple contexts and time periods to assess the overall weight of evidence and identify conditions under which the hypothesized effect holds or fails.

qualifier.temporal: during periods of rapid minimum wage increases (e.g., within 12 months of a significant hike)

C011.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with high labor demand elasticity
C011.object: informal sector employment and underemployment among low-skilled workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with high labor demand elasticity informal sector employment and underemployment among low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from developing economies (e.g., Indonesia, Brazil) tracking minimum wage changes and subsequent shifts in informal sector employment, with a focus on low-skilled workers during economic downturns. — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring the correlation between minimum wage hikes and informal sector outcomes under conditions of high labor demand elasticity and weak enforcement, controlling for macroeconomic shocks.

[PATH:literature] A meta-analysis of existing quasi-experimental studies on minimum wage effects in developing countries, specifically those examining heterogeneous impacts by labor demand elasticity and enforcement strength. — Synthesizes evidence across multiple contexts to assess whether the hypothesized effect is consistently observed, accounting for methodological differences and providing a more robust estimate of the direction and magnitude.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling using a search-and-matching framework with dual labor markets, incorporating endogenous firm compliance and worker sorting between formal and informal sectors under minimum wage policies. — Clarifies the causal mechanisms: if high elasticity leads firms to substitute formal workers with informal ones or reduce hiring, the model can predict conditions under which informal employment rises, offering testable implications for empirical work.

scope.domain: markets with high labor demand elasticity and weak formal sector enforcement

qualifier.geographic: developing economies with weak formal sector enforcement

C012.subject: Raising the minimum wage in markets with high labor demand elasticity
C012.object: positive effect on employment among low-skilled workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Raising the minimum wage in markets with high labor demand elasticity positive effect on employment among low-skilled workers]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of county-level minimum wage changes in U.S. states with high labor demand elasticity (e.g., retail, hospitality sectors) from 2000-2020, using synthetic control methods to isolate employment effects on low-skilled workers. — Directly tests the hypothesis by exploiting geographic and temporal variation in minimum wage policies within high-elasticity markets, controlling for confounding factors, and providing causal estimates.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies that explicitly stratify results by labor demand elasticity estimates (e.g., from Card & Krueger, Neumark & Wascher, and more recent work), focusing on low-skilled employment outcomes in the post-2000 U.S. context. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the hypothesized positive effect holds across multiple studies when conditioning on high elasticity, revealing consistency or heterogeneity in findings.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model incorporating monopsony power and labor demand elasticity, calibrated to U.S. low-wage labor markets post-2000, simulating the employment impact of minimum wage increases under varying elasticity assumptions. — Provides a mechanistic understanding of the conditions under which a positive employment effect could occur (e.g., countervailing monopsony), helping to refine the hypothesis and identify boundary conditions for empirical testing.
